title: Preface to Tatian: argue the soul without Scripture proofs
english: Most excellent Tatian, you asked me to send you a discourse and disputation on the soul, laid out with effective arguments and demonstrations, and in that matter to use no testimonies from the Scriptures. That way of teaching is true, and for those who want to think piously it is more certain and better fitted for proof than any human reasoning. Yet you want me to do it this way not so that you yourself may be satisfied — for you are already so formed that you cling to the divine Scriptures and to the traditions and constitutions, and you do not let yourself be moved from your conviction by any human reasonings — but in order to convince those who think otherwise, who refuse to give credit to the divine Scriptures, and who try, by a kind of skill in debate, to surround and deceive people unaccustomed to such disputes.

For these reasons I was led not to shrink from this treatment as if scared by inexperience, but, trusting your goodwill toward me, to obey your command and wish the more readily. You know, from your kindness and friendship toward me, how to bring into the light among people what is finely done, and how to pass over and cover what seems less rightly said. Knowing this, I have boldly set myself to write. I will use the order and method of arguing that those who profess such matters usually employ when they inquire with skill.

First, then, I will ask by what criterion the soul can be grasped according to its nature. Next, by what reasons it is shown to exist. Then, whether it is a substance or an accident. Next, whether it is a body or incorporeal. Further, whether it is simple or composite. Then again, whether it is mortal or immortal. Last, whether it shares in reason or is without it. These are the questions usually asked in a disputation on the soul as most proper to it, and as better marking out its force and nature. To prove and confirm what we must discuss here, we will use, as demonstrations, those common notions by which assent is usually won about things handled by the hands. For brevity and use we will now employ only those reasonings that most strongly demonstrate the matters under inquiry, so that, equipped with clear and easier notions and proofs, we may meet the gainsayers more readily. From this, then, let the beginning of our discourse and disputation be drawn.
